name: Endless rings
expr: (lambda p: None if p is None else [is_route(args[0], args[1], p, args[2], args[3]), len(p) - 1])(route(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2], args[3]))
show: five rings of 10, each joined to the next
why: Expected [True, 29]: a real route with 29 edges. The network has many cycles, so a vertex can be reached again and again. Mark a vertex when it is first reached, and never add it to the queue twice.

name: A path of 100,000
expr: (lambda p: None if p is None else [is_route(args[0], args[1], p, args[2], args[3]), len(p) - 1])(route(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2], args[3]))
why: Expected [True, 99999]: a real route with 99999 edges. A recursive search would go 100,000 calls deep, and Python stops at about 1,000. Breadth-first search uses a queue and no recursion.

name: 500,000 stops one step away
expr: (lambda p: None if p is None else [is_route(args[0], args[1], p, args[2], args[3]), len(p) - 1])(route(args[0], list(args[1]), args[2], args[3]))
show: 0 joined to 500,000 vertices; only the last one leads on
why: Expected [True, 2]: a real route with 2 edges. The queue holds 500,000 vertices at once. `list.pop(0)` moves every item left, so emptying the queue that way takes about 125 billion moves. `collections.deque` takes from the front in one step (lesson 2).
